To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we spectroscopically confirm a protocluster at $z$=2.23 with a total mass $M_{vir} \sim$ (1-2) $\times$ 10$^{14} M_{\odot}$.

the CC2.2 protocluster at $z$=2.2322 $\pm$ 1.01 is confirmed with 47 unique members, with a velocity dispersion of 645 $\pm$69 km s$^{1}$ and a total mass of (1-2) $\times$10$ ^{14}$ $M$ $_{\odot}$, and is expected to collapse and virialize to a Coma-type cluster by now.

we report the confirmation of a Coma-cluster progenitor at $z$~2.2 with a mass of $\sim$(1-2)$\times$10$ ^{14} $M_{\sun}$, and we show that narrowband surveys can be used to trace the large-scale structures at high-redshifts.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of galaxy evolution, star formation, and large-scale structure formation.
the study of galaxy formation and evolution, and the formation of the first structures in the Universe.
the study of the formation of large scale structures in the early Universe.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CC2.2 is a protocluster at $z$=2.23, with an estimated total mass of $10^{14}$ M$_{\odot}$ at $z$~2.2, and it is expected to evolve into a massive cluster at the present time.
CC2.2 is the most massive protocluster ever confirmed at $z$ $>$ 2, and it is the most massive structure ever confirmed at $1.8 < z < 2.4$.
CC2.2 is a progenitor of a Coma-like structure at $z$ = 0, with a total mass at $z$=2.2 of $M_{\rm vir} \sim (1-2)$$\times$$10^{14}$ $ M_{\odot}$.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have discovered the first Coma Cluster progenitor at $z$=2.2.
we can use the H$\alpha$ narrowband technique as an alternative to the Ly$\alpha$ narrowbands for finding protoclusters at $z$>2.5.
we have found a new protoclusters in the COSMIS field at $z\sim2.2$ with a total mass $\sim$ (1-2)$\times$10$^14$ M$_{\odot}$.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the large number of protocluster members we spectroscopically confirm at $z$=2.2 with a small amount of near-IR spectroscopic data, combined with a large narrowband imaging data set, can be used as a proof-of-concept for future surveys to trace the formation history of massive structures in the Universe.

protocluster members can be spectroscopically confirmed at $z$>2 using a relatively small number of masks with near-IR spectrographs on 8-10 m class telescopes, even in the case of a relatively low number density of protocluster members.
protoclusters at high redshifts can be identified and studied with relatively small amounts of spectroscopic resources.
